title: Minicolumns and Columns
intro: The word 'column' is used for at least two different things: the minicolumn, a thin vertical chain of about a hundred neurons, and the macrocolumn (or cortical column proper), a much wider cylinder that shares a receptive-field property. Knowing which one a model means — and how firmly the biology supports each — saves a lot of confusion when you read HTM, Thousand Brains or Blue Brain papers.

blocks.text: Picture the cortical sheet as a carpet. Seen from the side under a microscope, cell bodies in many areas line up in thin vertical threads running from L2 down to L6 — those threads are minicolumns. Now record with an electrode pushed straight down through the carpet: across all six layers, the neurons you meet tend to share a property, such as responding to the same patch of skin or the same eye. The region over which that property stays constant is a much wider cylinder — a column or macrocolumn — that contains on the order of a hundred or more minicolumns.

Lorente de Nó (1938) described vertical chains of cells as elementary units of cortical operation. Mountcastle (1978, 1997) gave the modern definition: a minicolumn is a narrow vertical chain of neurons, formed developmentally from the radial migration of cells along a radial glial fibre from the same region of the ventricular zone. Buxhoeveden & Casanova (2002) review the anatomy.

items: Neurons per minicolumn: commonly quoted as about 80–120, with roughly 2–2.5 times more in primate V1, which is unusually dense.

Width / spacing: centre-to-centre spacing is usually reported around 30–60 µm, with values from roughly 20 µm upward depending on species, area and measurement method (Nissl cell-body columns, bundles of apical dendrites, or myelinated axon bundles). Human values are often at the upper end; rodent and macaque values somewhat lower. Treat any single number as approximate.

Composition: mostly pyramidal cells plus interneurons; double-bouquet interneurons (often VIP- or CR-expressing) have narrow vertical 'horse-tail' axons that are thought to contribute to the vertical structure.

Related structure: apical dendrites of L5 (and L2/3) pyramids gather into bundles spaced about the same distance apart, the 'pyramidal cell modules' described by Peters and colleagues in monkey cortex.

blocks.text: A classic quantitative anchor is Rockel, Hiorns & Powell (1980), who reported a strikingly constant count of about 110 neurons in a 30 µm wide strip through the depth of cortex across several areas and species, with primate V1 the exception at about 2.5 times that. Later work challenged that uniformity: Herculano-Houzel et al. (2008) found neuron numbers under a unit of surface varying several-fold across areas in primates. So the 'about 100 neurons' figure is a good order of magnitude, not a constant of nature.

Mountcastle (1957) recorded from cat somatosensory cortex and found that neurons encountered in a perpendicular penetration all responded to the same submodality (e.g. light touch versus deep pressure) while oblique penetrations crossed between them. Hubel & Wiesel extended the idea to visual cortex with orientation columns and ocular dominance columns (Hubel & Wiesel 1962, 1977). Columns are typically quoted at roughly 300–600 µm across. For ocular dominance columns in macaque V1, each eye's stripe is about 0.5 mm wide.

In rodent primary somatosensory cortex, L4 contains discrete cell clusters called barrels, one per facial whisker, arranged in the same grid as the whiskers (Woolsey & Van der Loos 1970). A barrel column — the barrel plus the cortex above and below it — is a physically visible, functionally defined unit: its neurons respond best to its own principal whisker. Rat barrels are a few hundred micrometres across, and reconstructions put a rat barrel column at roughly 17,000–19,000 neurons; mouse barrel columns are smaller (several thousand neurons). This is the best biological justification for treating a column as a discrete module, and it is why so many quantitative circuit studies (and the Blue Brain reconstruction) use rodent somatosensory cortex.

blocks.text: The debate: is the column a real functional unit?
Horton & Adams (2005), in 'The cortical column: a structure without a function', argued that after 50 years no one had shown that columns are necessary for any computation. Their main points:

items: Column borders are often not discrete. Orientation preference changes smoothly across V1 with pinwheel centres; except for special cases like barrels, there is no wall between one column and the next.
Different columnar systems in the same area (ocular dominance, orientation, cytochrome oxidase blobs) do not align, so there is no single 'column' tiling.
Columns are variable within a species. Squirrel monkeys can have well-formed, patchy or absent ocular dominance columns, with no known effect on vision.

Some species lack them. Rats and mice have orientation-selective neurons arranged in a salt-and-pepper fashion with no orientation columns (Ohki et al. 2005 imaged this at cellular resolution in rat), yet their neurons are still orientation tuned.
Minicolumns are clear in some areas and hard to see in others; their functional role remains unproven.

blocks.text: The counter-view is that a column need not have hard borders to be a useful repeating motif: the local circuit (the laminar pattern of cell types and connections) is broadly repeated across the sheet, and whether functional maps are columnar may be a secondary consequence of how inputs are arranged. Most modellers today treat the 'column' as a convenient patch of a continuous sheet that contains the full canonical circuit, rather than as an anatomically bounded module. This is still an open question, and it is worth stating which version you assume.
How models use the two words

items: HTM (section 4): a 'column' in the Spatial Pooler and Temporal Memory is a minicolumn — a group of cells sharing feedforward receptive field, with several cells per minicolumn representing different temporal contexts. Typical HTM layers use 2048 minicolumns × 32 cells.
Thousand Brains (section 5): a 'cortical column' is a macrocolumn, about 1 mm² of cortex, that learns complete models of objects; each contains many minicolumns.
Potjans–Diesmann and Blue Brain (section 6): the modelled unit is a patch of cortex sized to contain the local circuit, with no internal minicolumn structure.
Diehl & Cook-style STDP networks: no columnar anatomy at all; the 'column' is just an excitatory layer with lateral inhibition, sometimes called a winner-take-all column.

blocks.text: What this means for your model

items: Name your units precisely. If your 'column' has 100 neurons it is a minicolumn-scale model; if it has 10⁴ it is a macrocolumn-scale model. Reviewers and future you will thank you.

A minicolumn is a sensible unit of shared feedforward input: give all its cells the same (or strongly overlapping) receptive field and let them compete or differentiate by context. This is exactly the HTM design choice.
A macrocolumn is a sensible unit for a sensor patch: one per receptive field or sensor, with its own L4/L2/3/L5/L6 populations and long-range lateral connections to other macrocolumns.

Don't hard-code isolation. Biological columns overlap and share lateral connections; a model of fully isolated columns that only interact through a final classifier misses the voting and context effects described in section 5.

Size budget: about 150 minicolumns × 100 neurons ≈ 15,000 neurons per biological macrocolumn. On a single GPU or neuromorphic chip, a few to tens of such columns at full density is realistic; beyond that, reduce cells per minicolumn or use point-neuron simplifications.
Treat the numbers on this page as ranges. When results depend on an exact cell count, sweep it.
